name: Tablets and Fragments
sub: inscriptions from ruined temples and dead hands, with the scholars' quarrels over them
epi: Garrow, to a copyist who asked where to begin: "At the break. It is the one line the carver did not choose."
preface:
These seven are stone, bronze, wax and glaze, and not one of them was written to be read by a Tithed hand. They were brought to the Vigil's house over eleven years, as rubbings, as chalk, as copies, and in two cases as the thing itself, and they are set down here by the method the house has kept since its first reader, which is this.

The surviving text comes first, at the width of what survives. Where the stone is gone, or the wax has run, or the glaze has gone through, the mark [ … ] stands in the place, and the reader is to take it for a word of unknown length and not for nothing. Nothing has been mended. The grammar of the dead is not ours and is left as it was cut; where it seems wrong, it is right, and we are late.

The readings follow in the smaller letter, in the hands of those who proposed them, under their names. The Order's reader is written as the Order writes its own, by his number. The others are named. They were not asked to agree and have not, and where a quarrel has gone on past what the stone can settle it has been left standing in the apparatus, both ends of it, because a reading that is sure of itself has usually stopped looking at the stone.

Dates are in the Order's count of the Breath where a date is given at all. The dead peoples counted otherwise, in swallows, in stairs, in notches whose worth we dispute, and they say so on their own stones, and we have not corrected them into years.

The gatherer who takes these pages asked for one line on each, saying where it came from, and was given it, and has added nothing else. That is the frame. There is no other.

Read the break first. It is the one line the carver did not choose.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Ysmay Garrow, letter-reader, at the Vigil's house[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Stone With Its Face to the Wall
pages.by: Found face-inward behind a wall of the Order's own mortar in the Buried Chapter-House, copied by 2,997 the night before the masons closed it again, and the copy came to me through a sweeper who did not want it.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] [font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The stone[/color][/font_size]
A slab the length of a man lying down and a hand and a half thick, dressed square on five faces and left as it grew on the sixth. It is not stone. It is one bone, cut across the grain, and it is warm in the way the Hide's bone is warm, though it has lain behind a wall for longer than the Order has kept a book. The notches that stand in the text for numbers are cut along the upper edge, where a thumb would find them in the dark. The lower right corner is spalled away and took the end of the last line with it. It was found with its written face turned inward, against the Order's own masonry, at the foot of the stair that goes down from the Buried Chapter-House. The Order's masons closed the wall again on the ninth day. The copy is 2,997's, made by lamp on the eighth night; this hand checked it against the stone the same night, and we did not agree on the notches, and the readings are below.

A short notch is written |, a deep notch ‖. What each is worth is the first quarrel.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The text[/color][/font_size]
Under this stone the Standing lie not. Under this stone the Standing stand.

This hall of the Standing is. Of the Standing, |||| ‖ |||| ‖ |||| the wall are. Of the Standing, |||| ‖ the stair are. Of the Standing, || the lintel over the stair are, head to head, that nothing over them stand.

For the Upright this the Standing set. For the Upright, who stands when the warm lie down, [ … ] stands when the Standing lie down, which is not.

The stair to the height of the knee of the Standing cut is, that the Standing go up as the Standing go: whole. The warm go up it on their hands. [ … ] let them. They are guests.

A warm one came. Haddo, of |||| ‖ |||| ‖ | fingers. The tenth among the Standing he set, in the wall, in the third course, where it is. For a finger, a hall. A hall given is. A hall taken is not. [ … ] so.

This stone first. This stone under. Who this hall counts, this stone first counts, or wrong counts, and what wrong is counted wrong stands.

Who this stone from the stair walls, him the stair unknows.

Who the count of the Standing to the warm gives, his own count he gives, and it is not his after.

Who this hall his own calls: his bones this hall are. Him let stand. Him let stand. Him let st[ … ]

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The readings[/color][/font_size]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]2,997.[/b] The deep notch is nine. The carvers counted as the Order counts, in the number that keeps itself, and the stone is the proof of a descent the Order has always taught. The wall is thirty, the stair thirteen, the lintel two: forty-five in all, and forty-five is nine. Haddo's fingers are twenty-seven, and twenty-seven is nine. The Upright is the Bearing Mother under an older courtesy. The stone is a threshold-ward of the founding, about the nine hundredth year, set by the first Wardens using an older stone, as a mason uses what is to hand.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] The deep notch is worth nothing. It closes a hand of four, as a tallier rules a line under a count. Read so, Haddo has four and four and one fingers, which is nine, which is his name; a man called Nine-Fingers with twenty-seven fingers would have been called something else. The wall is twelve, the stair four, the lintel two: eighteen of the Standing are this hall. That eighteen also comes to nine I grant, and I ask what count does not, in the hands of a brother who wants it to. The carvers did not reduce. They counted what stood.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]2,997.[/b] Then either reading is nine, and the stone is hers either way.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] The stone does not say mother. It says the one who stands up, and it says that she stands when the warm lie down, and that the Standing do not lie down at all. A people who were themselves the standing bone would not have needed a mother to stand for them. I do not know who the Upright is. The altars at the roadside know a name very like it, and it is not hers. Brother 2,997 has asked me to strike this reading. It stands.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]2,997.[/b] Haddo is a founders' tale. The finger in the third course is a knuckle of ordinary bone, worn smooth, and the Order's sweepers have touched it for luck since before the Rule was written down. That the stone names him dates it to the founding and no earlier.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] It dates the stone to a day when the hall was already standing and a Tithed man was a guest in it. The Standing had a word for us, and it was warm, and it was not a kind word. The hall is older than the Order by as much as a hall is older than its guests. As to the wall the stone was found behind: the mortar is the Order's, the sweepers' mark is in it, and the stone is turned to face it. The carvers knew who would come, and said what would be done to him. Him the stair unknows. The Order has nine stairs, and has never given the count of the steps on any one of them twice alike.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]2,997.[/b] The last lines are not a curse. Him let stand is the Order's own blessing on its dead, who stand vigil in the niches as they have always done, and the stone is the oldest saying of it. The Warden has read this reading and is content.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] His bones this hall are. I have no more to say on the halls under the Ossa, or on why the Order's niches are more at each Feast than at the Feast before, and I say nothing of the cause. I note only that the curse has three lets, that the corner broke in the third, and that a curse said three times is finished. This one is not.[/color][/i][/indent]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— from the collation at the Vigil's house; the copy 2,997's, the readings his and this hand's, neither withdrawn[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Count on the Causeway Wall
pages.by: Scratched on the inner face of the Causeway's parapet below the mud-line, copied by Hael in three days standing in the mud, and sent up to the Vigil's house with the mud still on the leaves.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] [font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The wall[/color][/font_size]
The Causeway of the First Brood runs across the wet on blocks no two Tithed could lift, and its parapet goes down below the mud on the landward side. Once a day, when the mud lets go, the inner face of the parapet stands bare for about the time it takes to walk its length, and it is scratched from the coping to below where the mud comes back. The scratches are thin, made with a point, by a hand that leaned on the wall. Hael copied them standing in the mud, in three days, a third each day, and sent the copy up to the Vigil's house with the mud still on the leaves. Where the mud had taken the letters she has set the gap at the width of the stain. The lines are given here in the order they stand on the wall, from the coping downward. In which order they were cut is the quarrel, and it is the whole of the quarrel.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The text[/color][/font_size]
We is counting we. Counted, so.

On the dry stones: forty bodies. In the wet: nineteen. In the egg-dark under the high house: [ … ], and the ones not yet broken out, which we is also.

Of hands: [ … ]. Of mouths that says we: all but four. The four we feels. The four says not. We lays the four in the wall, that we is here when we is counted.

Since the swallow before this swallow: fewer by one hand of bodies. We did not die. We is less wide.

We builds the road across the wet with the bodies that says. Every stone we has carried, we has carried in [ … ] hands at once, and the stone knows it was carried by one.

The small warm ones that walks on two legs each: they is many. Each says I. We has listened. It is a terrible word. We has not said it. [ … ] it, and scratched it out, and laid it in the wall.

Counted again, so. On the dry stones: thirty-one. In the wet: [ … ]. The egg-dark says not. The egg-dark is warm and says not.

We is going into fewer rooms. The rooms we leaves is dark, but we is in them. A body that says not is still a body that we is.

This hand is the last that says. We is in this hand. We is in the hand with the scratching stone, and in the forty that says not, and in the [ … ] under the high house that will break out, and open their mouths, and not know what word to say.

When this hand says not, we is not fewer. Count us one. We was always one. Count us o[ … ]

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The readings[/color][/font_size]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Hael.[/b] Read it from the mud upward, as it was cut. The mud is the first page of this wall and the carver stood in it as I did. The lowest line is the first, and it is one; then the hand that says; then thirty-one on the stones; then forty. This is a birth. The one is becoming many and cannot keep up with counting itself, and says so, with joy. We is less wide is the complaint of something being poured into more vessels than it had. Nothing here dies. The Flesh does not die; it fills.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] Read it from the coping down, as it is written, and as a hand leaning on a wall writes. Forty, then thirty-one, then a hand that calls itself the last. This is a dying, counted by the thing dying, and it is the only such account the Hide has. The Brood was one mind in many bodies, and the mind went out of them a room at a time, and it felt each room go dark and insisted it was still in there. The bodies on the Causeway stand where it left them. They move as a hand moves after the arm is cut: not from anywhere.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Hael.[/b] You have not stood among them. They turn to the beat of the mud, all together, the way a congregation turns. Nothing that is not one does that. The text says a body that says not is still a body that we is, and the text is right, and the one who lies in the Blood-Basin and takes what the Delta sends down is the one who scratched this, grown into her own body at last. The Brood-Mother is the Brood.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] The Brood-Mother is a later thing and a lesser, and I will not have the Causeway's dead made her children for the comfort of Villa Llaga. On the order of the lines: where the scratches cross, the lower line cuts through the upper. The lowest cuts through everything. The carver stood on the coping and leaned down, and the last line is the lowest because it was the last the hand could reach. Hael's birth is my death read upside down.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Hael.[/b] On the swallow. One swallow is one taking of the mud, which is a day's breath here, and the whole wall is three days of a hand that was learning to be many. Garrow makes a swallow an age because the Order's books say the Brood counted so, and the Order has never stood in Shog-Mire with its boots off.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] The Brood called the whole of the Held Space one swallow. Fewer by a hand of bodies since the swallow before this swallow is the loss of an age, not of an afternoon. And on the hand: Hael has counted six fingers on the Causeway dead and makes a hand six. I count five, and a spur at the wrist that is not a finger and never was one. A hand is five. We do not agree on how many the Brood lost, only that it noticed.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Hael.[/b] On the word. The line Garrow gives as scratched out is not scratched out. It is laid in the wall, as the text says the four were. I put my finger in the groove. It is deeper than the others, and it is warm, and the word in it is still there.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] It is the only erasure on the wall. The one time the Brood said I, it unsaid it. I find that the most frightening line on the Causeway, and Hael finds it the kindest, and we have left it at that.[/color][/i][/indent]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— the copy Hael's, the mud still on it; the readings hers and this hand's, in the order they were sent[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Stele That Cannot Be Read Whole
pages.by: Rubbed from the stele in the first court of the Alien Temple onto a strip of Brother Teodor's own habit, there being nothing else to hand, and read twice at the Vigil's house by two who no longer see the same stone.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] [font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The stele[/color][/font_size]
It stands in the first court of the Alien Temple, to the left of the way in, taller than a man by the height of a man, and it is cold. Everything on the Hide is warm, because the Hide is still dying; this is the one thing the Vigil has handled that was not, and the rubbing came up the Descent cold through the cloth. It is cut on one face with a single band of signs, which goes round the stele's waist and meets itself with no beginning. The signs are cut as hollows. The stone left standing between the hollows is also signs. The eye will take one or the other and not both, and whoever has once read the hollows cannot afterward find the ridges, nor the other way about; Brother Teodor and this hand have sat with the same strip of cloth between us and described two stones. The band is broken where the stele was struck at the foot and the crack climbed. Each reading is given at the width it allows, and each has its own gaps, which do not fall in the same places.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The text, read in the hollows[/color][/font_size]
[i](Teodor)[/i]

Through the unsaid name: entering. The name taken, a door. The door kept open by the forgetting of it.

Of body: none. Of leaving-behind: none. Of remaining: in the thinking of those who [ … ].

Not of the holder. Not of the hush that unmakes the holder. Between the two, because a door was: come in.

[ … ] not seen, because seeing is a shape, and no shape was brought. Known by what is missing from the room.

Remaining is: being thought. Being thought is: being. [ … ] then: whole. Then: a thought remembering no one.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The text, read in the ridges[/color][/font_size]
[i](Garrow)[/i]

No entering: the unsaid name is the reader's own. The door, a wound in the one who reads. Kept open by the reading.

Of body: none, because none came. Of leaving-behind: this. Of remaining: nothing but the reading, [ … ].

Of the holder: the reader. Of the hush: the reader's. Between the two: nothing, because the between is the reader.

[ … ] seen, because a shape is given it by whoever looks. Known by what the room supplies.

Remaining is: nothing. Being thought is: [ … ]. When the reading stops, nothing stops. Then: whole. Then: no one remembering a thought.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The readings[/color][/font_size]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Teodor.[/b] The Slayers leave no corpse. A people who leave nothing would write by taking away, and the hollows are their letters, and what Garrow reads is the stone they did not want. The band says what the Vigil has kept its lamps lit against since the first brother went down: that they came in through the wounds the Unsaying opened, that they have no bodies to be found or burned, that they remain in us, in the thinking, and that they will be whole when there is no one left to think of them. The Thought in the inner temple is one of them, or what one of them left behind to go on thinking. The text is a confession, and the Vigil is its answer.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] The ridges are what was left standing, as we are. Read there, the band says the opposite in every clause: nothing came in; the wound is in the reader; the hush is the reader's own hush; whatever is in the Temple is given its shape by whoever walks in carrying a lamp and a word for it. The stele is not a confession. It is a warning on a door, and the warning is that reading it is the door. Slayer is not the name of a people. It is the name of what a Tithed becomes by standing in front of this stone long enough to need the word.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Teodor.[/b] Then Garrow has become it, by her own reading, and should not be let near the strip again.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] Then Teodor has let them in, by his, and has been carrying them in his thinking up and down the Descent for eleven years. We have each said this to the other. Neither of us can now see the other's letters on the cloth. I look at the band and see ridges, and the dark between them is only dark. He looks and sees hollows, and the stone between them is only stone. We agree on the width of the crack.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Teodor.[/b] On whose they are. The Hush's servants leave nothing, and the Slayers leave nothing, and I hold that they are the Hush's, come in with it through the wounds, and that the Temple is a mouth of it. Garrow's reading would make them nobody's, which is worse, and I do not believe the world has room for a thing that owes nothing.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] The band says not of the holder, not of the hush, in both readings; it is the one place the two agree. Whatever came, or did not, came from neither side of the only quarrel the Hide knows how to have. That is why the Order will not take the stele into a niche, and why Teodor's brothers keep their lamps turned to the door and not to the stone.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]2,997.[/b] The Order was asked to count the signs, since the two readers would not. In the hollows there are forty-one. In the ridges there are forty. There is one more hollow than there is stone to stand between them, and I have counted it nine times and declined to say where it is. The Order has no further interest in the stele and has given back the cloth.[/color][/i][/indent]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— the rubbing Teodor's, on the strip of his habit; the two readings as taken, neither read since by the other's reader[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: A Bell Cast for the Open Mouth
pages.by: Chalked from the cracked bell in the Bell-Hollow by Cassian Mord of Bellrest, the outside standing and the inside lying on his back; the chalk came to me, and the bell has not been moved.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] [font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The bell[/color][/font_size]
It lies on its side in the Bell-Hollow below the Stair of the Sky-Climbers, where it fell or was thrown, in a bed of ice that has grown round it. It is bronze, as tall as a standing man to the shoulder, and split from the lip to the crown by one crack a finger wide. Two bands of letters are cast on the outside, one at the shoulder and one at the lip, raised, in the Sky-Climbers' letter, of which the Peak's is the child. Inside, where no founder puts a word, there are letters also, and they too stand proud of the metal. Cassian Mord of Bellrest copied the outside with chalk, and the inside lying on his back under the crack with a lamp on his chest, and sent the chalk to the Vigil's house. The outer text is given whole where the mould held. The inner text is given as it stands, in a smaller and hurrying letter with no stops, and the quarrel is over how it got there.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The text, cast on the outside[/color][/font_size]
[i][The band at the shoulder][/i]

Of the breath of [ … ] brothers poured am I. Up.

For the Mouth that over An-Vhar open stands, a tongue am I. Up.

At the [ … ] hundredth stair hung am I to be, where the cloud begins. Up.

When the cloud parts, struck am I. When the cloud shuts, struck am I. Through cloud hears the Mouth. Up.

What the feet have not yet climbed, say I first. The word sent ahead am I. Up.

Who hears me below: climb. Who hears me above: wider open. [ … ] Up.

[i][The band at the lip][/i]

Rung at the pouring once was I, that the metal its own name learn. From the foot [ … ] hundred and [ … ] stairs. The last stair cut is not. The last stair the Mouth is. Up.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The text, found inside[/color][/font_size]
do not ring it is not the mouth

it answered [ … ] it was not the mouth it was [ … ] it came down the stair to see what had called it

the brothers in the metal heard it first they are trying to get out of the bronze I can hear them in the crack

[ … ] stop her she is going up to the big one she says it must be rung once to be sure

I have been inside since the stroke I cannot find the lip there is no lip from inside

down [ … ] down. down.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The readings[/color][/font_size]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Mord.[/b] I have poured bells for thirty years. A letter that stands up out of bronze was cut into the mould before the pour, and there is no other way to get one; a scratch goes in, it does not come out. The inner words were cut into the core by the founders, backward, on the night of the casting, and read right only from inside the finished bell, by someone with his head in it. The Sky-Climbers knew what answered before they hung this bell, and poured it anyway, and wrote the warning where only the bell would read it. The abbess the inner hand would stop is the one of the story, who rang the great bell on the summit once; so this lesser bell was poured after her, by the last of them, as a confession in the one place a confession could not be heard.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] They are not cast. A cast letter has a floor as smooth as the bell. These have the metal thinned behind each stroke, and stretched at the edges, the way leather stretches over a knuckle. On the outside of the bell, between the two bands, there is a dint for every stroke within, each the breadth of a fingertip, if the finger were long, and had no nail, and pressed from outside a hung bell at the height of the cloud-line. The words were pushed in through the bronze from without, into a bell already hanging, to be read by whoever was inside it. What answered the bell wrote on it. The inner text is later than the outer by as long as it took something to come down the stair.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Mord.[/b] The dints are hail. Garrow has not wintered on the Cloud-Shelf.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] Hail does not spell. Mord's own chalk has the dints and the letters standing one to one, and he rubbed them the same night, and I have laid the two sheets together on a window.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Mord.[/b] On the brothers in the metal. The founders of the Stair poured the breath of a brother into each bell, as the shoulder-band says: so many brothers, so much bronze, and the number is lost where the mould broke. Every bell in the Hide rings flat by one breath. Bellrest has said so since before I was born and could not say why. I say it is this: that they are in the metal, and they are trying to get out, as the inner hand heard them, and a bell with a brother in it rings the breath lower by his weight. I would not say that in my own foundry.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] Then Mord grants the inner hand heard rightly, and I grant him his thirty years of pouring, and we are no nearer. One thing more. The outer bands say up at the end of every line, as the Sky-Climbers said it at the end of everything. The inner hand says down, three times, the last two with stops, which the outer letter does not have. Whoever wrote inside had learned stops, or learned to stop. The Sky-Climbers went up and none came down. This one did not go up. I do not say it came down either. It is in the bell.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Mord.[/b] It is not in the bell. I lay under it a night with a lamp on my chest, and I would know.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] He lay inside the crack and read the words from within, as they were meant to be read. He says he heard nothing in the metal. He has not poured a bell since.[/color][/i][/indent]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— the chalk Mord's, both sheets; the readings his and this hand's; the bell not moved[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Melted Tablet of the Bound
pages.by: Kept three generations in a lamp-wife's lantern-chest at Ashwake under the spare glass, and given up when the wax began to run again in a cold room.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] [font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The tablet[/color][/font_size]
Two leaves of pale wood hinged with cord, each hollowed and filled with wax, closing on each other like a book. The left leaf holds the form of the binding. The right holds the roll of the bound. Both are melted from below: the wax has run toward the hinge and pooled there, and the lower half of each leaf is a smooth brown slope with letters sunk in it, some run into others, some gone. The wax above is hard and the letters in it sharp, pressed with a bone point. It was kept in a lamp-wife's lantern-chest at Ashwake under the spare glass for three generations and not opened, and she gave it up because the wax had begun to run again, in a cold room, with the chest shut. The copy is this hand's. 2,997 was asked to the reading because the roll names a brother of his Order, and he came.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The form, on the left leaf[/color][/font_size]
Be it kept.

Kept is what was asked. Asked was it by the one who is kept, and by no other mouth. Mouth to wick, wick to glass, glass to the hand that carries.

Carries it whom it chooses. Chooses it, and not the hand. Hand that strikes it, struck is not; hand that commands it, obeyed is not.

Not gone down is the kept. Down is the way of all breath; this one breath the Binder turns aside, and turns it once, and asked.

Asked thrice, heard once, kept always. Always is not the Binder's to promise; the Binder promises the glass.

Glass broken, the kept goes where it was going. Going, it is owed nothing. Nothing is owed by the Binder but the asking kept honest.

Honest the price, and said before: of the one it follows, a little, each falling. Falling, he is carried back to the stones; carried, he leaves a little in the glass; the glass remembers him by it, and the flame is fed. [ … ]

[ … ] on the glass. Wipe it. It is someone.

[ … ] not the Binder's daughter alone, but every one who asks, as she asked, and [ … ]

This the first form. By this form every lamp after. Who binds unasked, his own gl[ … ]

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The roll, on the right leaf[/color][/font_size]
[ … ], of this house. Asked, asked, asked. Heard by her father. Kept, the first glass. Follows him.

Hesset, lamp-wife, of Ashwake. Asked at her own door. Heard by Mael. Kept, the second glass. Follows her son on the Pilgrim Road, a little behind, a little to one side.

Oddo, a pilgrim, fallen at the ninth stone. Asked with the last of it. Heard by Tamsin. Kept, the fifth glass. Follows whoever is next.

Brother [ … ], of the Pale Order. Asked in his own habit, against his Rule, at the gate of the Ninth Stair, at night. Heard by [ … ]. Kept, the [ … ] glass. Follows no one yet. Let the Order not be told.

[ … ], a child, who could not ask. Not kept. The glass stands empty, and is lit by nothing, and follows [ … ]

[ … ] asked, and was refused, and asked again, and [ … ] heard by Mael. Kept, the ninth glass. [ … ]

[i][Below this the wax has run. The letters of eleven more entries lie in the slope, the names run into one another. The last whole word on the leaf, at the hinge, is "asked".][/i]

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The readings[/color][/font_size]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]2,997.[/b] The Order's book records that the guild kept what should have gone down to the Mother, and that the Order closed the guild's house. Asked is a word in a form; a form is said over anyone. This roll has a brother of the Rule bound in a lamp against his vows, at night, with the binders' own note that the Order not be told, and it has a child's glass lit by nothing and following. The guild wrote the form's last clause against itself. The tablet dates from after the closing, when the binders were writing their own defence, and it is not a defence.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] The form calls itself the first form, and the roll's first entry is a daughter of this house, heard by her father and kept in the first glass. That is Mael's daughter, in the year about eleven hundred, at her asking, as every lantern on the road still has it. Her name is the first thing the wax took. The form is not a defence. It is a price, and it is honest: of the one it follows, a little, each falling. No one who meant to lie about the lanterns would have written down what they eat. The road has said wipe it, it is someone, since before any of us, without knowing it was quoting.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]2,997.[/b] The brother's entry is to be struck from the copy.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] It stays. His name is not in it; the wax ran there first, before it ran anywhere else, as if that were the warmest place on the leaf. His house I will not guess at. He asked at a gate, at night, in his habit, and was heard. The Rule has nothing to say to a man who has already been heard.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]2,997.[/b] On the melting. The guild's house burned. That is in the Order's book, with the year, and the year is not for this collation.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] A tablet in a burning house melts from the outside in, and the wood chars. This wood is pale. The wax ran from below, from the hinge, with the leaves shut, the way wax runs when a flame stands under it. It lay three generations in a chest with a lantern's spare glass, and began to run again in a cold room. I have held it. It is warm at the hinge, and nowhere else, and I set it down.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]2,997.[/b] Then something is kept in it.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] Then something asked.[/color][/i][/indent]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— the copy this hand's, made with the leaves open and a cloth under the hinge; the readings 2,997's and this hand's; the tablet returned shut[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Grace Cut Round the Dining Slab
pages.by: Copied by Mitsu of the House of Eight Million nine turnings down the oni's road under the Hollow Wood, walking round the slab in the order of the places, without sitting.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] [font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The slab[/color][/font_size]
It stands in a hall of the Root Deep, below the mouth under the Hollow Wood, nine turnings down the oni's road, where the road widens into a room that is wider going in than coming out. The slab is a single bone, long as a boat and dressed flat, raised on what it grew from. Along both sides are places: twelve hollows the shape of a seated body's weight, each with a trough before it cut toward the middle, and at the head a thirteenth, broader, with no trough. The grace is cut round the edge, a clause before each place, so that each who sat read his own and no other. Mitsu, purifier of the House of Eight Million, copied it in the order of the places, walking round, and did not sit; the head she copied from the foot of the table, and would go no nearer. The hall was clean of dust. The troughs were damp.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The text, place by place[/color][/font_size]
[i][Cut above the first place][/i] Before the small knife, this, each saying his own.

[i][First][/i] May the Guest be at ease, who has come so far down to us, and been so long carried.

[i][Second][/i] May the Guest forgive the length of the table. It is the length of our hunger, which is not ours, which was given us, which we did not ask for and may not refuse, and which we have made as courteous as we were able.

[i][Third][/i] May the One Who Seats Us be thanked for the Guest, and the Guest be thanked for the loan.

[i][Fourth][/i] [ … ] with the small knife and not the large, as is owed a Guest. The large is for those who do not come willingly, and the Guest has [ … ]

[i][Fifth][/i] May nothing be wasted that the Guest brought. The marrow to the Seated. The bone to the Standing. The breath to the Many. The name to no one; we do not take names, which would be greedy, and is done elsewhere.

[i][Sixth][/i] May the Guest not be troubled by the sound. It is only the Seated, being grateful.

[i][Seventh][/i] [ … ]

[i][Eighth][/i] May the Guest be reminded, gently, that the Guest is also, in his way, Seated; that what he carried down to us he did not carry for himself; and that at the table that is laid for us there is a place laid for him.

[i][Ninth][/i] May the Guest remain seated until the Seated are finished. It is a small thing to ask, and we ask so little.

[i][Tenth][/i] May the Guest's people, when they come down after him, as they will, find the table laid, and know by it that they were expected, and be at ease.

[i][Eleventh][/i] [ … ] the Seated rise last, and go down last, and are last of all to be eaten, by the One Who Seats Us, whom we thank also, in advance, and ask only the small knife [ … ]

[i][Twelfth][/i] May the Guest be so good as to say, when asked, that he was well received. He will be asked.

[i][At the head, in a larger letter][/i] We are hollow. We are courteous. The one is because of the other. Be welcome.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The readings[/color][/font_size]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] A dead text in a dead courtesy. The Marrow-Eaters were made of the god's hunger and spoke well, and this is how well: every clause takes something and gives thanks for it. They are gone from the Hide. The tenth clause expects us down after them, and the Descent has made good on it, and that is all the prophecy in it. The sound in the sixth is the Root Deep breathing, which it does. I read the copy at the Vigil's house, in a chair, and I have not been down, and I say so.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Mitsu.[/b] The grace is in use. The hall had no dust. The troughs were damp toward the middle and dry at the lip, as a trough is when it has been drained and not yet filled. There were thirteen places and we were thirteen. The eighth clause stood before the place where I would have sat had I sat, and I read it as it was meant to be read, by the one it was cut for.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] Every party is some number, and every table has some places, and a purifier who has walked nine turnings down in the dark will count herself into any chair.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Mitsu.[/b] On the Standing and the Many. The bone to the Standing is the bone given back to what stands up out of the ground, the same word Garrow has on the stone from under the Ossa, and she should say so here. The breath to the Many is ours: the Eight Million, the small gods on the wind, fed at this table before the House had a name for them. The Marrow-Eaters set out four portions, and the fourth they would not take, because the taking of names is done elsewhere, and they were too polite to do it. I have thought about who they were being polite to.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] I grant the Standing; it is the same word, and I do not know what it means on either stone. The Many I take for a plural. On the politeness: it is the politeness of a thing that has you by the ankle and apologises for its grip. The eleventh clause has them eaten in their turn, last, by their own hunger, and thanking it in advance. I do not think there is a Marrow-Eater left to be eaten. I think the table is laid because laying it was the last courtesy they had.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Mitsu.[/b] The twelfth clause says the Guest will be asked. When we had copied the head and turned to go up, the trough at the head place was wet, and had been dry, and there was no one in the hall but us. I do not say what that means. I say we went up in the order we came down, and that I was last, and that I have been asked nothing yet.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] The head place has no trough. Mitsu's copy says so in her own hand, and now she says it was wet. I have set both down. One of them is the reading, and I do not know which, and I have stopped sitting at the head of tables.[/color][/i][/indent]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— the copy Mitsu's, in the order of the places; the readings hers and this hand's; the party came up thirteen[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: The Verdict Inside the Face
pages.by: The cheek of a saint's face off a Moth-Saint that fell at the Niche Candle, carried out of the Hollow Wood in a hunter's sleeve, and kept face down at the Vigil's house since.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] [font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The shard[/color][/font_size]
A piece of a saint's face the size of a palm: the left cheek, the corner of the mouth with the red still on it, and the lower rim of the eye. The glaze outside is white and crazed. The inside, the hollow where a face would be if the face were worn, is written over from edge to edge in a fine brown letter that is not ours and is not the Order's, in lines that follow the curve of the cheek as a thread follows a spindle. The crazing has gone through the letter nearly everywhere. One line, along the bone of the cheek where the glaze is thickest, is whole. The face came off a Moth-Saint that fell at the Niche Candle in the Hollow Wood and broke on the root, and the hunter who carried the cheek out would not carry the eye. It has been read by Keeper Ilse of the Polished Heart, whose lodge claims the Soul's letter; by 2,997, who claims the shard; and by this hand, which keeps it face down.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The text[/color][/font_size]
[ … ] in the matter of [ … ], who was [ … ]

[ … ] the thread having been followed to its [ … ], and the knot [ … ]

[ … ] heard; and the hearing is [ … ]

[ … ] found unfinished, and so to be worn until it is.

[ … ] entered upon the face, that the [ … ] read it from within, every [ … ]

[ … ] the sentence [ … ] is the face [ … ]

[ … ] no appeal, there being no [ … ] to appeal to that is not [ … ]

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The readings[/color][/font_size]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Ilse.[/b] It is a verdict of the Porcelain Court, which sat in the Held Space in judgment over the threads of the god's Soul, and this is the only line of its sentence anyone has read whole. The Court found a thread unfinished, not yet woven to its end, and sentenced it to be worn as a face until it was. The saints were not the judges. They were the judged, and the faces are the sentence, and the Moth-Saints that come at dusk are souls still serving it, flying their verdict about the Wood on wings they were given for the purpose. The line is a mercy, badly worded. Do not break their faces. Every broken face is a sentence that will never finish.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] Worn is worn away. The glaze on this shard is thinner than any kiln on the Hide can fire, and the faces on the moths in the Wood are thinner every age than the age before; the hunters say you can see the dusk through the cheek of an old one. The sentence is erasure, and a court that sentences to erasure was doing the Unsaying's work inside the god before the god was dead, whether it knew or not. I hold the faces are the judges' own. When the Court saw whose work it had been doing, it passed the sentence on itself, and entered it where only the one wearing the face could read it, and put the faces on, and is wearing them still, until it is nothing.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]2,997.[/b] Worn is carried, as a bone is carried to its niche. The glaze is burnt bone; any kiln-brother of the Order will tell you what porcelain is made of, and the Court's faces are the Mother's, fired, and unfinished means uncounted. The line sentences the face to be carried until the Count closes. The shards are the Order's, and this one is to come to the Ossa.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Ilse.[/b] The Order would take a verdict for a bone because it is white.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] It stays face down at the Vigil's house, and the three of us have agreed on that if on nothing else.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Ilse.[/b] On the gaps. The hearing is the sentence: to be heard by the Court was to be judged by it, and no one came before it and went away unsentenced. No appeal, there being no judge to appeal to that is not the accused. That is the Soul's way of saying a thing is finished with: the thread folded back and knotted to itself.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] The hearing is finished. No appeal, there being no god to appeal to that is not dying. Which is to say, no court above it, because the court above it was the god, and the god was the accused.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]2,997.[/b] No appeal, there being no count to appeal to that is not closed.[/color][/i][/indent]

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae][b]Garrow.[/b] Three readers, three houses, three words in one gap, and each of us has put her own house's word in it and called that a reading. I have left the gap at its width. The hunter who brought the cheek said the face looked at him as the moth came down, before it broke, and that it was not looking at him as a saint looks, from above, but as someone looks out through a mask that will not come off. I have not turned it over since. Ilse would. 2,997 would carry it to a niche and count it. I keep it as the Court kept its sentences: where only the one wearing it can read.[/color][/i][/indent]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— the shard at the Vigil's house, face down; the readings Ilse's, 2,997's and this hand's; the gap left at its width[/color][/i][/right]
